extracted.intended_audience: general readers and literary/historical readers; aspiring editors of small literary periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles embedded in a memoir about running a small literary/transcendentalist periodical (The Dial), plus related practices (use of a journal in political canvass; organizing women-only conversations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal as essential tool in a political canvass
rubrics_metrics.description: To put a good, efficient journal into the hands of every voter who will read it is the true mode of prosecuting a political canvass; meetings and speeches are well enough, but this is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: $1,000,000 raised by open subscription and judiciously, providently expended in furnishing information touching the canvass to the voters of New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania. Emphasizes targeted distribution of an effective paper over reliance solely on meetings/speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial principle: 'A perfectly free organ'
rubrics_metrics.description: "A perfectly free organ is to be offered for the expression of individual thought and . character. There are no party measures to be carried, no particular standard to be set up. A fair, calm tone, a recognition of universal principles, will, I hope, pervade the essays in every form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dial's stated editorial aim: independence from party lines, openness to individual thought, calm/fair tone, recognition of universal principles. Further: the journal should aim not to lead public opinion but to stimulate each person to judge for himself and to think more deeply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone rule: avoid dogmatism and avoid compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: "I trust there will be a spirit neither of dogmatism nor of compromise; and that this journal will aim, not at leading public opinion, but at stimulating each man to judge for himself..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should strike a balance: avoid imposing dogma while refusing mere compromise; prioritize stimulating independent judgment rather than attempting to direct public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure influence by fit audience, not circulation numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: "I presume the circulation of The Dial never reached two thousand copies, and that it hardly averaged one thousand. But its influence and results are nowise measured by the number of its patrons, nor even of its readers. To the 'fit audience, though few,' ... it was like manna in the wilderness; and scores of them found in its pages incitement and guidance to a noble and beneficent... career."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small circulation does not imply small impact; evaluate a periodical by depth of influence on the right/fit readership and by the lasting effects on its readers, rather than raw circulation figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and objectives for women-only intellectual conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of conversations (in Boston) for women only, wherein she was to take a leading part; but every one who attended was required to contribute according to her ability, by written essay or spoken word, as should be suggested or found possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic objective: to answer 'What were we born to do?' and 'How shall we do it?' (or 'to vindicate the right of Woman to think'). Topics drawn upon included Life, Literature, Mythology, Art, Culture, Religion. Attendance was small (averaging less than fifty), contributions expected from attendees, and the exercises intended to stimulate serious thought and practical self-education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy/style tradeoff: loftiness and force may trump clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: On 'Woman in the Nineteenth Century': 'If not the clearest and most logical, it was the loftiest and most commanding assertion yet made of the right of Woman to be regarded and treated as an independent, intelligent, rational being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work of advocacy may be judged effective for its moral force and loftiness even if it lacks strict clarity or logical precision; editors/reviewers should weigh rhetorical power and inspirational reach alongside analytical clarity (noting the author cautions that gaining in clearness might reduce force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and financial viability tied to sales
rubrics_metrics.description: "The original editor was to have been paid a salary of two hundred dollars per annum, had the sale of the work justified so liberal a stipend; but I believe it never did."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial pay and sustainable staffing for a small periodical are contingent on sales/revenue; plan budgets and compensation with realistic circulation expectations.
